doc.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Playing in the Haney Brothers carnival showboat band
summary: Ousley tells of a few months with a carnival band, still dates, fair dates, the slow train and prejudice on the last car.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Now I read in something that you played for quite a number of years in a circus band.

Yeah, well that was only really not — it was only for one year — in fact not a whole year, for about four or five months. I joined a carnival, Haney Brothers. And I think I joined it in Champaign, Illinois. And of course the carnival plays cities, and usually on the outside or the outskirts of town. And they called that a still date. Because at that time it’s only the carnival there and it usually started say about six o’clock in the evening after people get off from work. And they’d come out on the carnival. And we had what we called it was a showboat. And it was supposed to be like a showboat on the Mississippi River. And it was a tent, but in the front we had a ramp you would come up like you would do on a boat. And we would play, we were on the balcony playing, I don’t know how many people, about seven people in the band. And then of course we had — the entertainers would be on the bottom deck. And then we had what we called a barker. And what he would do on the midway, say like if a crowd of people are down here, the barker © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

for that particular show would come out and he’d let the people know what they’re going to see. Well as soon as that show let out, if your tent was next then you had to be there to catch those people. And you’d bring them to your site. And of course when they got to us the barker would tell them — and then he would say a lot of things that was not true, like we got the girl that does the dance of the seven veils and she’d drop these veils one by one. Then the girl that does the dance with the balloons or bubbles and you punch — and they were never on the show. And so the carnival is a place usually where the entertainers there are either entertainers that have been in the business a long time but are no longer at the top of the business, they’re not working as much, so the carnival offers work, or they’re young entertainers like myself trying to get started. So you don’t make no money on a still date. The only time you make money is doing the fair dates. That’s when you go to the cities where the farmers are selling their livestock and they have auto races, and the carnival is there. So they have a lot of people. And you work pretty hard. Like we would get on the midway at nine o’clock in the morning, and our last show would be at one o’clock in the morning. And so we would end up doing about 25 shows. But the carnival, it was a lot of fun, there was some hardship and a lot of times with no money but there’s still a certain something about it. You know like they say the sawdust in your vein kind of thing. There are things about it that you enjoy. But in the case of the carnival that we were at, I guess after I was on there a month, about two months, I said well I’m going to have to get back towards — the money was very short sometimes. So I said well the next time I get train fare, I’m going, I’m leaving. So that’s what happened a lot of times. I think I left in Muskogee, Oklahoma. But I traveled around, I saw a lot of things. In fact we had a trumpet player on there named Frank, he played two trumpets at one time. And he used to drink a lot. And so sometimes he’d throw the trumpet up, and a few times he missed it, and his trumpet was all bent up. You know, but it was a lot of fun, there was a lot of love there, and hard times, but it was a mixture of a lot of things. It was a good experience.
I wanted to make sure I understand what you meant by “steal dates.” Is that what you said?
Still date. Well still date probably meant there’s not a lot of activity.

The carnival, like I say, we would get started about six o’clock in the evening when people would come home from work. But there wouldn’t be a lot of people out there. And so we might close down at around ten, just depending on how many people you had. So you didn’t make a lot of money. And the Haney Brothers had a train, that we rode on. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-
But we used to joke about the train, that it was so slow you could get off the train, go to the store, get something to eat, come back and catch it.

And again, even on there there was a certain amount of prejudice. Because we were on the last car. But it was really like family. We had the turtle lady on there, the turtle lady, she even had her boyfriend.
